segments.text: Our course operations engineer needs to read a report in a separate AWS account,
and the request to assume the reporting role succeeds; the application still
receives an access error because it continues sending its original
credentials, so a successful role assumption did not change the identity of
that application.
There are two boundaries to understand: permission to enter the role, and
permission to perform work with the resulting session; we will separate those
decisions, repair a cross-account trust mismatch, then fix the application that
acquired the right session but never actually used it.
You only need the distinction between an identity and an allowed action to follow
this lesson; temporary credentials are the short-lived proof that a caller presents,
while the role describes an access arrangement, not a second password that
permanently turns the engineer into an administrator.
The Security Token Service can return temporary credentials for an assumed role,
including an access key identifier, a secret access key and a session token;
software must use the complete set together, rather than treating the token
as optional or combining a new token with an old secret.
The response also identifies when the credentials expire, which gives the
session a limited lifetime but does not turn every application into an automatic
renewal system; a supported credential provider can obtain fresh credentials,
whereas values copied into a long-running process can simply become stale and stop
working.
Do not expose those values in a lesson, source file or support message while
investigating a failure; use identity and expiration information for diagnosis, and
store or obtain credentials through the approved mechanism for the workload, with
the same care you would apply to any other usable secret.
In the reporting account, the role's trust policy identifies the allowed caller and
any required conditions for assumption; its permissions policies describe the
service actions and resources available through the role, so granting report
access does not by itself invite the engineer from another account to assume
that role.
The engineer's account must also authorize the cross-account assumption request for
the intended role; this is our two-sided example, where the caller's permission and
the target's trust must agree, rather than a universal statement that every
same-account trust arrangement always needs an identical pair of policies.
Conditions and other applicable controls can still limit either request, and an
explicit deny is not repaired by casually adding another allow; establish whether
the failed operation is role assumption or the later report read before changing a
policy, because they are different requests evaluated in different contexts.
In the first worked repair, the engineer's permission points to the intended report
role, but that role trusts an obsolete operations identity; the assumption
request fails before a report read is attempted, so increasing access to the
report bucket would change the wrong boundary and leave the immediate problem
unresolved.
Check the intended caller, exact target role and required trust conditions with
both account owners, then correct the narrowly scoped mismatch in the target
trust; do not replace the principal with everyone or remove meaningful conditions
simply to make the test pass, because the repair must preserve who is allowed in.
Repeat the assumption through the approved source identity and confirm the returned
session belongs to the expected role in the reporting account; also verify an
unintended caller remains rejected, then test the required report operation
separately, because successful entry still does not prove that the data permissions
are right.
Follow the successful path in three stages: the engineer starts with an
authorized identity and requests the target role using the supported access
mechanism; this produces a role session, but it does not silently rewrite every
open terminal, running service or saved application configuration on the
engineer's computer.
The process making the report request must select the intended role-based credential
source, allowing its supported provider to perform assumption and refresh where
configured; the details depend on the tool, so verify the tool's documented
credential selection rather than assuming that the last command run controls every
other program.
Check the identity seen through that same credential path, then perform the minimum
required report operation and a relevant disallowed operation; the combined
evidence establishes which caller made the request and whether its access is
appropriately scoped, instead of relying on a green role-assumption message from
another terminal.
In the second worked repair, the engineer obtains a reporting session in one command
but starts the application with its old profile, so the application never uses the
returned access; repeating role assumption or granting the original identity broader
report permissions would hide the configuration mistake instead of fixing
it.
Inspect the credential source selected by the application and configure its
documented role profile or provider for the intended target, removing unintended
conflicting sources through the approved configuration process; different tools
resolve credentials differently, so do not blindly delete every environment setting
or assume one precedence rule describes all software.
Run the identity check through the corrected path and retry the report
request with the application itself, confirming the expected reporting role and
account; then verify an unrelated write remains unavailable, preserving the
read-only boundary rather than calling the repair finished because the application
can now do almost anything.
For a command-line diagnostic, the STS get caller identity operation reports the
identity associated with the credentials used for that call, including account and
identity information; invoke it through the same profile or credential path as the
failing request, because a default-profile check can describe a different caller
entirely.
Seeing the expected role identifies the caller but does not prove permission to
read the report, and this diagnostic does not require a normal allow permission for
its own operation; do not mistake a successful identity lookup for evidence
that a restrictive role policy has stopped working or grants broad service access.
Record enough non-secret information to distinguish the account and session in the
investigation, then validate the intended data operation and applicable
restrictions; keep credential material out of logs, and avoid treating a friendly
session name as proof of authorization merely because it resembles an approved
person's name.
The engineer may have wide responsibilities in the original account,
but the reporting session is not the union of those original permissions and the
role's permissions; after assuming the role, the service request is made through
that session and its applicable access rules, which is why a deliberately narrow
reporting role is useful.
A session policy supplied during assumption can narrow the permissions
granted through the role's identity policies, not expand them beyond what the
role grants there; other applicable policies and resource grants still need
correct evaluation, so the simple intersection is a useful boundary model
rather than a complete diagram of every IAM case.
When the correct role still cannot read the report, inspect its intended action
and resource along with relevant conditions and restrictions; keep this
investigation separate from trust, because proving the caller may enter the role and
proving the resulting session may read a particular object are different pieces of
evidence.
For the AssumeRole operation, session duration is bounded by the role's
configured maximum and the operation's rules, with a maximum role setting of
twelve hours; requesting a longer value does not override that configuration, and
a remembered duration from a different token operation is not a reliable rule for
this request.
Assuming another role with existing role credentials is role chaining, and that
chained session is limited to one hour through the command line or interface; a
larger target-role maximum does not remove the chaining cap, so diagnose the source
credential type before changing the requested duration repeatedly.
Ordinary console role switching is not automatically the same credential chain as
consecutive programmatic assumptions, because the console uses the original
sign-in credentials to authorize its switches; use the documented behavior of
your actual access path, and plan supported refresh instead of choosing the
longest possible session as the only reliability measure.
Workforce federation lets an organization use its external identity system to
support controlled AWS access rather than creating a permanent IAM user for every
employee; authentication at the external system and the mapping into an allowed AWS
role are related stages, not evidence that every signed-in employee should receive
the same permissions.
A browser identity token is not interchangeable with the temporary AWS
credentials used to sign service requests; the supported federation mechanism
performs the appropriate exchange and checks, so do not paste a website token
into a secret-access-key field or treat successful website login as proof of
report-bucket authorization.
Follow the organization's supported workforce access arrangement, including
its authentication requirements, role assignment and session handling; the
operational goal stays the same as our course example: the intended person
reaches the intended role, and the actual request is made with the resulting
authorized session rather than an unrelated cached identity.
Suppose a third-party reporting service operates for many customers, including the
course team, and assumes a role in each customer's account; an external ID helps
prevent the provider from being confused into using one customer's role for another
customer's request, a different problem from ordinary employee sign-in
authentication.
The provider assigns a customer-specific external ID and supplies it during
assumption, while the target trust checks the expected value alongside the trusted
principal; it is not a password or secret, and knowing it should not replace being
the correct trusted caller with the required authorization and narrowly scoped
role access.
Verify that the provider's intended request works and requests with a missing
or incorrect value do not, without exposing usable credentials in the test
record; an ordinary console role switch cannot supply this external-ID
requirement, so use the supported assumption path rather than removing the
condition to make a console shortcut work.
Our final check starts at entry: confirm the intended source can assume the exact
target role with its required conditions, while an unintended source cannot; this
validates the cross-account agreement without relying on report access as an
indirect and potentially misleading test of who may enter the role.
Next establish the actual caller used by the report application, not just a
separate terminal, and confirm its account, role and valid session lifetime;
if identity differs, repair credential selection first, because additional report
permissions would conceal the wrong caller and weaken the architecture we meant to
build.
Complete the check with the needed read and a meaningful disallowed operation,
plus a supported refresh path for continued use; this leaves the team with a
verified reporting workflow and a repeatable diagnostic sequence, instead of
a collection of broader permissions added each time an access error appeared.
The reporting failure is now repaired at both boundaries: the right source may
enter the target role, and the application actually uses that role session; temporary
lifetime, federation and external IDs refine this access path, but none replaces
checking the identity and permissions of the request that reaches the service.
Next we examine IAM analysis tools, including credential reports and access
activity that help a team review what it still needs; subscribe to From Bytes Up
for clear AWS lessons that connect identity evidence to careful access
decisions, without treating a quiet usage report as proof that every permission can
be removed.
